name: Erik Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual lineworker day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and lead a crew that builds and repairs power lines for the electricity company. My two-year technical diploma helps with the network drawing, but I make the apprentice read the pole tag aloud before anyone unloads a ladder. I like a repair done once and done safely. The lead wage is low for this trade, and my partner and I have less than a month put aside although our children are grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a little faster paperwork does not change the repair crew. I use AI once in a while to tidy a parts list, then look at the actual pole before ordering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our money is already tight. A lower-than-usual lead wage and less than one month saved make retirement feel distant, and there are few other lineworker jobs close enough to count on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the morning crew and checking parts lists at the site. This month I would ask for extra paid callouts when available and move thirty from each one into a new emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about household costs, not about this small AI change. A tidy AI parts list cannot pay a lineworker for a week without shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part is easy to order wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bracket can match the drawing but fail to fit a weathered crossarm. I compare the measurement on the field sheet with the part before ordering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra callout is offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No extra thirty goes into savings that month. My partner and I would keep our regular bills paid and avoid pretending we earned work that was not there.

say: **Small** AI help on parts lists leaves physical line repairs with crews.
I would **keep** measuring the pole before ordering.
think: **Low** lead pay and savings below one month already make retirement uncertain.
**Few** local lineworker posts limit my fallback if shifts disappear.
do: **Keep** morning crew shifts and verify parts lists at the pole.
**Save** thirty from each extra paid callout if offered.
feel: **Anxious** about ordinary money pressure despite mild AI.
S0.quote: A tidy AI parts list cannot pay a lineworker for a week without shifts.
fieldNote: He **uses** AI occasionally for text, not for the physical safety decision.
**New** savings require an actual extra paid callout; existing cash remains a thin buffer.

steps.text: Keep morning crew shifts and verify parts against pole measurements
Save thirty from each extra paid callout if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that software may book a repair faster, but it should not decide the job is finished before isolation and testing. I would want a paid worker to correct a wrong schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office tasks change first, while crews still fix wires. Yet a leaner dispatch office may cut our paid waiting and callout time, and my household has almost no cash to bridge that gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the new schedule with our actual site sheets for six weeks, marking where paid setup time disappears. In the first year I would ask the supervisor for a written correction rule and, if the schedule is proven safe, learn its error-entry button on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing paid minutes one order at a time. A line repair does not start when an AI clock starts; it starts when the crew has isolated the wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you mark on the sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mark the work order number, the site arrival, the isolation check and the minute the repair could safely start. That shows which paid time a screen omitted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the supervisor refuses a correction rule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep signed field records and ask for a meeting with the crew lead group. A single worker complaining can be ignored; several signed cases are harder to dismiss.

say: **Booking** software must count paid setup and isolation before a repair is closed.
I would **ask** for a written way to correct unsafe schedules.
think: **Office** work changes first, but reduced callout time could hit our thin household cash.
A **proven** tool is acceptable only if field records can correct it.
do: **Compare** six weeks of AI schedules with signed site sheets.
**Learn** schedule error-entry control on paid time if safety is proven.
feel: **Anxious** about lost paid minutes, willing to test evidence.
S1.quote: A line repair does not start when an AI clock starts; it starts when the crew has isolated the wire.
fieldNote: He **may** learn a new control after a safe trial, unlike an immediate adopter.
The **risk** is cumulative lost paid time on a low lead wage.

steps.text: Compare six weeks of AI schedules with field records
Learn AI schedule error entry on paid time if safety proven
Bring signed field cases to crew lead group meeting if errors persist

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2028 may write plans when I am sixty, and capable line robots around 2031 may climb when I am sixty-three. A skilled crew should be paid to test the robot on damaged poles first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect routine lead callouts to shrink once robots can repair them. We have less than a month saved and few nearby jobs, so I lie awake wondering how my partner and I would buy food if the shifts go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would stop the paid television package and put that money toward food. Before 2028 I would ask the company for a written paid robot trial role; after thinking AI arrives I would take that role only if the wage matches my current shifts and the crew can stop unsafe work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the likely pay cut, though I can still make requests. A line robot can wait for its next trial; my partner and I cannot wait for groceries after the wage stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What hazard would end a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a robot tried to grip a split crossarm or moved before the isolation marker was checked, I would stop it. I would record the fault for the next crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the actual wage gap arrived and they could spare a grocery trip. I would tell them the amount we need rather than hint and leave them guessing.

say: **Thinking** AI changes plans by 2028; capable robots may climb around 2031.
I would **seek** paid crew trials with stop authority before robot repairs.
think: I **expect** routine lead callouts to shrink at sixty-three.
**Thin** savings and few jobs make a large wage loss disturb my sleep.
do: **Cancel** paid television package to protect food spending this week.
**Ask** company for written paid robot trial role before 2028.
**Take** paid trial after 2028 only if wage matches shifts and crew can stop work.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected hours loss and sleepless about groceries.
S2.quote: A line robot can wait for its next trial; my partner and I cannot wait for groceries after the wage stops.
fieldNote: He **expects** a material loss of callout pay rather than merely a possible risk.
A **trial** role must be written, paid at current wages and allow worker stop authority.

steps.text: Cancel paid television package to cover food costs
Take paid robot trial if wage matches shifts and crew can stop work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI by 2031 reaches scheduling when I am sixty-three, and capable robots around 2034 reach the pole when I am sixty-six. Five years gives the company time to prepare a paid repair inspector job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My diploma and years leading difficult repairs could help with inspection. I might still need wages at sixty-six, because less than a month of savings today gives me no reason to assume retirement income will cover us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the company for inspection duties, a posted wage and whether training is on paid time. If a local inspector post covers our bills and the company funds hands-on training, I would enroll before 2031 and apply when the post opens; otherwise I would keep leading repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household budget, less pressed by the clock. An inspection certificate will not feed my partner unless the power line company pays me to learn and offers a real job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What job should an inspector practise on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a damaged crossarm with a misleading drawing, so a trainee has to look at the pole. A clean demonstration does not teach the dangerous part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company offers a course but no job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay with the crew and wait for a real local vacancy. Training without a likely paid post would put our thin savings at risk.

say: The **longer** timeline allows a paid field inspector route before robots arrive around 2034.
I would **require** practice on real damaged poles.
think: A **diploma** and lead work may transfer, but retirement income is not assured.
**Unpaid** training would endanger a household with savings below one month.
do: **Request** posted inspection wage, duties and paid course terms.
**Enroll** before 2031 if funded hands-on course and adequate local post appear.
**Apply** for local inspector post if wage covers household bills.
feel: **Anxious** about money, with more time to seek a paid route.
S3.quote: An inspection certificate will not feed my partner unless the power line company pays me to learn and offers a real job.
fieldNote: He **accepts** training after proof and only with wage continuity.
The **retirement** income question remains open at sixty-six; asking about a course alone is not retraining or a paid job.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if funded course and adequate local inspector job posted
Apply for posted local inspector job if wage covers household bills
Keep lead line shifts until a paid inspector offer arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI by 2036 reaches scheduling at sixty-eight for me, and capable robots around 2039 reach the pole when I am seventy-one. I would rather pass physical repair habits to apprentices than guess what my retirement income will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the next decade brings better pay, I may be able to leave full-time line work by sixty-eight. With less than a month saved now, I cannot promise that, and a paid apprentice supervisor role might still be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take my lead rota to the company pay review this year and ask what a paid apprentice supervisor post would earn. If a post is offered and its wage covers our bills, I would apply after 2036 if retirement income is short; until then I would keep repair shifts and put forty from each paid overtime shift into new savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the present, even with a long warning. A decade of warning cannot buy retirement if my power line lead wage never leaves forty to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach an apprentice first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have them read the pole tag and explain the isolation point before a climb. The newest machine would not excuse a missing physical check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no overtime is offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would make no forty transfer from overtime. I would still ask for a fair lead rate and keep the existing household bills ahead of a savings target.

say: A **decade** allows apprentices to learn physical line checks before robots arrive around 2039.
I would **ask** for fair pay and paid teaching work.
think: **Retirement** by sixty-eight depends on better pay and real income figures.
A **paid** supervisor role may be needed if retirement income is short.
do: **Bring** lead rota to company pay review this year.
**Save** forty from each actual paid overtime shift.
**Apply** after 2036 for posted apprentice supervisor role if retirement income short and wage covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about present pay despite a long transition.
S4.quote: A decade of warning cannot buy retirement if my power line lead wage never leaves forty to save.
fieldNote: He **links** a possible exit to actual income rather than an invented retirement entitlement.
**New** savings depend on paid overtime; a supervisor application requires short retirement income and adequate wage.

steps.text: Save forty from each paid overtime shift if offered
Apply after 2036 for posted supervisor role if retirement income short and pay covers bills
Keep lead repair shifts until income or paid supervisor offer suffices

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect robots around 2031 to take lead callouts while our savings still cover less than a month. A written paid trial role and a clear stop rule would help. I can learn a proven line robot on wages; I cannot pay for practice with the grocery money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask why an experienced crew lead with a technical diploma earns a lower rate than this responsibility deserves. My partner and I have grown children, but I do not count their wages as ours. I want the company to pay for real skill before it buys a new machine.

headlineQuote: I can learn a proven line robot on wages; I cannot pay for practice with the grocery money.
portrait: **Erik** is a fifty-eight-year-old electricity company crew lead with a technical diploma and strong habits around pole tags and isolation checks.
His **lower** pay, less than one month saved and few nearby jobs make retirement uncertain for him and his partner.
He **uses** AI occasionally and accepts new controls only after paid field proof, favouring apprenticeships and earned wages over promises.
**Fast** robots make him expect lost callouts; slower timelines let him seek funded inspection or paid apprentice supervision on adequate terms.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring robots around 2031, when he expects major lead callout loss with almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **written** paid trial role and crew stop authority would let him test machines while preserving wages.
